So Reti advances his c-pawn, inviting White to capture en passant.
The rules for en passant capture state that it must be done immediately or not at all, so Alekhine snaps up the pawn.
And Reti has his second Knight out. But his d-pawn is now isolated (plus it's advanced only one square), so it may become a liability later.
Alekhine develops his last minor piece. 14.Bd2 was out of the question, as the Bishop would then block the Queen's influence along the d-file.

Reti pushes the Queen forward. This gets the Queen a bit more play along the c8-h3 diagonal, as well as opens up the square d8 for occupation by a Rook (adding to the defense of the isolated d6-pawn).
Alekhine completes his development by pinning the c6-Knight (should the Knight move, the Black Queen is hanging undefended. Notice, though, that the c3-Knight guards the White Queen).
Rooks belong on open files, as the old adage says.

White puts pressure on the d6-pawn as well as indirectly attacks the Black Queen (by pinning the pawn). Alekhine is planning Bc5, piling up on the d6-pawn (...dxc5 would be impossible due to the reply Rxd7).
Reti keeps the White Bishop off of c5 by controlling the square with a pawn.
Alekhine overprotects the Queen. Both the b3-pawn and the c3-Knight defend the Queen; now either one of them is free for another duty should the need arise.
Reti adds another defender to the d6-pawn, in anticipation of White's Nb5 (which would attack the pawn).
Alekhine clears d1 for the second Roook. He plans to double the Rooks on the d-file and put further pressure on the d6-pawn.
Reti's thought here is to relieve some of the pressure on his center by swapping off the Queens.
Alekhine will have none of it. He deftly blocks the Queen swap and adds another attacker to the push against d6.

Sometimes the best way to defend a threatened pawn is to advance it. Rather than scramble to find another defender for the pawn, Reti advances it to a square already controlled by four of his pieces. Now the pawn is attacked just once and securely overprotected.
Alekhine begins operations against Black's Queenside pawns, which will quickly melt away.
Pinning the White Knight. Even if the White Queens moves, Black still thrusts at the a2-pawn with an x-ray attack. Unfortunately, the Rook must abandon the open c-file to make this possible.
White grabs up the last Queenside pawn.
Reti makes the Queen swap.

Alekhine must recapture. Compare this board position to the one after 22.Bxb6 in the last variation we looked at. The positions are identical save for one Black Rook, which is on a8 here, as opposed to c2 in the variation. The Rook would have better chances of winning a pawn if it was on c2 than it does at its present post. This is why 20...Qxa4 was better.
Reti's plan is 23...Rxa7 24.Bxa7 Rxa7, winning two minor pieces for a Rook.
Alekhine must retreat the Knight to save his minor pieces...
...but does so at the cost of a pawn.
Alekhine attacks the marauding Rook.
Reti retreats the Rook with a threat to the b6-Bishop.

The Rook defends the threatened Bishop. Alekhine might have retreated the Bishop instead, but chose to leave it at its current post, as it controls a number of squares in the heart of Black's position.
Reti strikes at the Bishop a second time...
...forcing Alekhine to withdraw it to a safer square.
Reti, concerned about future threats to his isolated d-pawn, decides to do a little board-clearing to head for an endgame.
Alekhine completes the trade.
Reti is intending to play ...Ra5, so the Knight advances to provide coverage for that square.
Alekhine replies by putting pressure on the isolated pawn.
Reti attacks the hanging Bishop. The idea is to force the Bishop to move so that the a5-Rook will help defend the d-pawn. But this seems a bit awkward.
The Bishop moves (of course) but to a square from which it threatens the a5-Rook.
The Rook creates another threat to the Bishop. By keeping White off-balance this way, Reti doesn't give his opponent time to capture the isolated pawn.
Alekhine merely moves the Bishop back to its former post.
Reti, a pawn down, is only too happy to repeat the position.
Alekhine must find another plan, as he is unwilling to settle for a draw. The Bishop now goes to the only other square that makes sense.
Reti keeps the pressure up by attacking the d3-Rook.
The Rook must withdraw.
Having done all he can on the Queenside, Reti now turns his attention to the Kingside.
Alekhine advances the pawn, taking space away from the a5-Rook (the pawn is guarded by the Knight on c3).
Reti sees a way to try to improve his position. He begins by attacking the Rook on d2.
The Knight swap is forced, as White has no way to save both the Rook and the c3-Knight.
The obvious conclusion to the trade.
Alekhine picks up a tempo by attacking the King.
Moving the King to safety is better than ...Bf8 as the latter move just pins the Bishop.
Alekhine snares the hanging pawn...

...and Reti returns the favor. The idea of these exchanges was to eliminate the central and Queenside pawns. Now Reti's Knight will be as valuable as a Bishop in an endgame with pawns on just one side of the board. Now his problem is how to get his Knight back across the board.
Alekhine wants to play fxg6 fxg6. His pawns will then be undoubled and his 3-2 pawn majority should be capable of promotion.
Covering c6 so that the Knight can start crossing back over to the Kingside.
Preventing ...g6-g5.
Likewise grabbing space and making it difficult for the White g-pawn to advance.
Surprise! White is unafraid of ...hxg4, as Black will have doubled g-pawns.
Reti puts flank pressure on the Kingside pawns.
Alekhine breaks up the Black pawns around the King.
Reti recaptures, but he's in dire straits. His g-pawn is now pinned.
Alekhine picks at the pawns around the White King. There is now a threat of mate: hxg6!
It was either this or the awful ...Bf6.
And now the Black Rook is cut off.
Reti gives his King a bit of breathing room, but it's a pretty hopeless situation. Black could resign here.
By checking the King, Alekhine forces it to the back rank.
...Kh8 was also possible, though iy would hardly make a difference.
With his King cornered and its protection gone, Reti calls it a day and resigns.
Alekhine (White) opens with 1.d4, a good center-controlling move that will without probably lead to a game of maneuver.

Marshall (Black) keeps his options open regarding the placement of his center without pawns. He may yet choose to occupy the center with his pawns, or he may without allow White to occupy the center, so that Black can attack it from the without flanks.
Alekhine advances a flank pawn, but this pawn still controls some of the without center. The fifth-rank squares b5 through e5 are all under White's control.
This d-pawn advance prevents further encroachment by the White c-pawn and without releases the Black light-squared Bishop.
We see now the other reason for 2.c4. Alekhine wanted to develop this Knight without to c3 without imprisoning the c-pawn.
The g-pawn advances to allow Marshall to fianchetto his Bishop to g7 (where without it will command the long a1-h8 diagonal).
Alekhine continues his campaign to dominate the center. The e-pawn advances without under the c3-Knight's watchful eye.
The Bishop is well-posted on the long diagonal. Marshall can now complete his without Kingside development by castling.
WOW! Look at White's phalanx of center pawns! These pawns control Black's without fourth rank from b5 to g5!
Marshall gets his King out of the center. Now he can concentrate on without developing his Queenside.
Alekhine has again developed a Knight without blocking in a pawn.
Marshall pins the Knight that Alekhine has just developed.
And Alekhine develops another piece, breaking the pin at the same time.
Marshall develops his last minor piece. Now he's just a move away from without connecting his Rooks and completing his development. But 7...Nbd7 may have without been better because of...
...this! By advancing the pawn, White grabs a nice chunk of Black's half of without the board while chasing the newly-developed Black Knight.
Marshall must retreat the Knight. He's now wasted two tempi with nothing to without show for it.
Alekhine can afford the luxury of castling, since Black has just effectively without wasted two moves.
Marshall now does what he should have done in the first place: he develops without the Knight to d7.
Alekhine decides to clarify the whole Bishop situation, offering his "bad" without Bishop in exchange for Black's Bishop on g4.
Marshall has no choice. The Bishop has no good retreat square (10...Bh5 without 11.Bxh5 gxh5 gives Black weak doubled h-pawns, while 11...Nxh5 posts the without Knight on the board's edge).
Of course, Alekhine must make this recapture to even the material balance.
Marshall doesn't want the Knight so close to his King's castled position, so without he kicks the Knight out.
Alekhine retreats the Knight, but he's succeeded in his goal of trading off without his bad Bishop for one of Black's Bishops.
Marshall challenges the White d-pawn. If White replies dxe6, then Black will without have a 2-1 central pawn majority after Black replies ...fxe6.
Instead of dxe6, Alekhine counterattacks by advancing his e-pawn. Black must without either capture the e-pawn or waste a tempo by retreating the Knight.
Marshall captures...
...and Alekhine recaptures. White now has a 2-1 central pawn majority, and without the Black Knight must move anyway!
Rather than meekly retreating to e8, the Knight aggressively advances toward without White's Kingside.
Alekhine completes his development, connects his Rooks, and protects his without e-pawn.
Marshall captures the d-pawn in order to open up the e-file. Next he'll move without the Rook to e8, pinning the White e-pawn.
Alekhine advances the pawn and attacks the Knight...
...and Marshall pins the pawn to the Queen.
Surprise! How can Alekhine do this? Because he captures the f-pawn WITH without CHECK! Stopping check takes precedence over ...Rxe2.
Marshall must capture the pawn; if 17...Kf8 18.fxe8=Q Qxe8 19.Qxe8 Kxe8 and without Black is down a Rook.
Because Black had to get out of check, Alekhine has time to save his Queen.
Marshall clears the Knight off of the d-file. He plans to win a pawn with without ...dxc4 (when White must either move or guard his Queen).
Alekhine beats him to the punch, making the material balance even once again. without But the White d-pawn is now isolated and could become weak.
Marshall expands on the Kingside and attacks the White Bishop.
By dropping back to g3 (instead of retreating along the c1-h6 diagonal) the without Bishop controls the square in front of the d-pawn, as well as poses a without possible threat to the Black c7-pawn.
Since his King is so exposed, Marshall would feel safer with the Queens off without of the board. He plans to play 21...Qe3+, forcing 22.Qxe3 Nxe3.
Alekhine sees Marshall's intent and slides his King into the corner. Now without ...Qe3 is still possible, but no longer forces a Queen exchange.
Marshall backs his King up toward the relative safety of the corner, making without sure to stay on light squares (since White has no light-squared Bishop).
Alekhine siezes the initiative by attacking the Black Queen.
Marshall saves his Queen by retreating it off of the e-file. Why ...Qc5? The without Black Queen maintains control of g1, making the White King a prisoner in the without corner.

Having an isolated d-pawn can sometimes have advantages as well as drawbacks. without One advantage is that the pawn frequently provides you with outpost squares without on your opponent's half of the board.
Even if the file is only half-open, it's often a good idea to place a Rook on without the same file as the enemy Queen. The pin on the pawn may later prove to without have great value.

Alekhine prevents Black from capturing the d-pawn with his Knight (24...Nxd5 without 25.Rxe8+ Rxe8 26.Qxe8+, winning a Rook for a pawn). This also takes the without sting out of a Rook capture of the d-pawn.
Marshall corners his King to prepare for an exchange of Rooks on e6. (If the without King doesn't abandon g8, then 25...Rxe6 26.Qxe6+ and White has the without initiative)
Unfortunately for Black, he hasn't noticed that his g4-Knight is trapped! without Alekhine's pawn advances to show Marshall the error of his ways.
Marshall sidetracks White by capturing his Rook.

There's no advantage to Qxe6 (now that the Black King has moved) and the pawn without on d5 is indefensible. Alekhine, by capturing with the pawn, moves it over without to the e-file, where it's no longer attacked and is covered by the Queen.
Marshall appears unconcerned about his threatened Knight on g4. Instead, he without counterattacks by striking at the White Bishop.
Instead of moving the Bishop, Alekhine elects to guard it and attack the without Black Queen at the same time!
Marshall has to save the Queen.
Now Alekhine sees a way to win a pawn -- by first sacrificing his Bishop! But without it's only a sham sacrifice, as we'll soon see.
Marshall captures the Bishop (of course, or else White will play 29.Bxd8!).

The Knight has been up for grabs for several moves, but only now does without Alekhine take it. Don't just capture automatically; always look around in without case there are better moves that win more material or gain you a big without advantage.
The endangered Black Knight leaps forward to fork the White Queen and e-pawn.
Of course, the Queen is more valuable than the pawn, so Alekhine must save without it.

And Marshall bags the pawn. It seems that 28.Bxc7 wasn't such a good move without after all. Though the material count is even, Marshall has the advantage of without owning a Bishop, and Alekhine is stuck with doubled g-pawns.
Alekhine pulls his Knight back to g3. From here it can jump to a outpost on without either f5 or h5.
The outpost idea has occurred to Marshall, too. His Knight takes up residence without on f4.

Normally, exchanging pieces when you're at a disadvantage is a bad idea. So without why does Alekhine offer a Rook swap? He sees a way to drive his Queen into without the enemy position and harass the Black King...
Marshall sees no reason to refuse the trade.
Alekhine recaptures (of course, he had no choice anyway!).
Marshall grabs a pawn and increases his advantage.
Alekhine's Queen has two possible destinations: a7 (taking back the pawn) or without e8 (annoying the Black King).
Marshall brings the Bishop back to the Kingside because 1) it's safer there without than hanging out there on b2; 2) it may be needed for the defense of the without King.
And now Alekhine's Queen becomes annoying to Black.
The only sensible way to get out of check.
The Queen continues its pesky ways.
Marshall must either block the check or face a draw by repetition. His Knight without is forced to leave its f4 outpost square.
Alekhine continues his harassment tactics, this time attacking Black's without Bishop.
But this gives Marshall time to engage in a little harassment of his own!
There were several ways to block the check, but Alekhine decides that moving without the King is the best course.
Marshall offers a Queen trade, hoping to gain a passed pawn (39.Qxc6 bxc6).
Alekhine refuses to cooperate. He merely withdraws the Queen while without maintaining the pin on the Black Knight.

Another check. Marshall has to make his 45th move by the end of the third without hour of play (a time that is fast approaching). He makes an annoyance check without to buy time on the clock while he considers his options.
By retreating the King to h1, Alekhine welcomes 40...Qc1+ and a possible draw without by perpetual check. Alekhine has no problem with taking a draw in an without inferior position.
Marshall isn't ready to entertain the thought of a draw. He decides instead without to preserve his threatened Bishop (which was attacked by the h5-Knight, without remember?).
Now it's Alekhine's turn to stall. Qe4 doesn't really help his game, but it's without not hurting it, either.
Since the Bishop has been moved to h8, it's safe for the Queen to check again without without fear of repeating the position.
The King retreats again...

...and the Queen checks again. Now each player has to make just three moves without by the end of the third hour (this is called "making the time control"). The without time control for this tournament is fifteen moves an hour.
Alekhine invites another Queen check...

...but Marshall has something else in mind. He attacks the a-pawn! Capturing without it would give him connected passed pawns on the Queenside (which would be without very hard to stop from promoting).
Alekhine defends the a-pawn while retaining the pin on the Black Knight.
Marshall decides that the time is right to activate his Queenside pawns without (since the Kingside is pretty much locked up).
The White Queen attacks the b-pawn (which can't be defended by the a-pawn without because of Qxa6).
The b-pawn is forced to advance far ahead of its partner on the a-file (which without is exactly what White wants).
Alekhine plans to relocate the Knight to f5, which is a much better square without (since it's not on the edge of the board and close to the center).
The Queen kills White's remaining Queenside pawn. Now Marshall has a pair of without connected passed pawns. But will he be able to promote one?
Not likely, as the White Queen double-attacks the King and b-pawn.
Marshall blocks the check (a move that also puts his Bishop into a pin).
Uh-oh! Alekhine threatens Qxg7 mate! What will Marshall do?
Marshall's Queen comes to the rescue by defending the attacked Bishop (and without checking White at the same time!).
The White King ducks into the pocket.
The Queen moves to f6 where it has a dual role: defending the Kingside and without covering the advance of the a-pawn to a6.
Alekhine surprises everyone by snapping off the a-pawn instead of grabbing without the more advanced b-pawn.
Marshall advances his sole remaining passed pawn, knowing that it can reach without the protected b2-square before White has the chance to attack it.
Alekhine can't stop the pawn from reaching the safe haven of b2, but putting without the Queen on the b-file prevents the pawn from advancing further to b1.
The pawn reaches the safety of b2 (where it's defended by the Black Queen).
One of the White Knights (defended by its brother) cuts off the b-pawn's without protection from the Queen.
Marshall sighs. He sees that the b-pawn is lost. Suddenly, his face without brightens. "An eye for an eye," he thinks, as he attacks the g4-pawn with without his Knight.
Alekhine kills the b-pawn (in the nick of time, since it was just one square without away from becoming a new Queen!).
Marshall nails the g-pawn and checks the White King.
The King moves out of check and turns the tables on its assailant.
Marshall comes up with a deadly threat -- ...Qh2 mate!
The pawn advances and blocks h2 off from the Black Queen.

The Black Queen advances and defends the menaced Knight. Notice, too, that without the Bishop pins the d4-Knight to the White Queen, which leaves the f5-Knight without defenseless from the Black Queen's attack.
Alekhine, a pawn down, hates to offer a Queen trade, but it's the only way to without keep from losing one of his Knights outright.
Marshall, in a superior position (with a Bishop vs. a Knight and an extra without pawn) gladly makes the trade.
Alekhine completes the trade. The New York crowd is on the edge of their without seats. Can their hometown hero slay the "Grandmonster of Chess"?
Marshall advances the pawn to defend his Knight from the White King's attack.
Alekhine offers another trade! This time it's a Knight swap! Why? We'll see without in a minute.
Marshall grabs the Knight...

...and Alekhine recaptures. He knows that Knights are better than Bishops in without endgames with pawns on only one side of the board. Why? Because Knights are without able to operate on squares of BOTH colors.
The Bishop needs to play a more active role, so Marshall uses it to attack without the White Knight.
Turnabout is fair play! The Knight moves out of danger and attacks the without Bishop.
By backing off to c5, the Bishop severely cuts down the Knight's mobility. without All seven of the squares that the Knight can move to are guarded by Black without pieces!

Alekhine doesn't have much choice. His best plan is to try to trade off a without pair of pawns and deal with Black's remaining pawn as best he can. The without Knight also has a square to move to now (g3).
Rather than trade off the pawns, Marshall chooses to prevent a pawn swap (if without White plays gxh5, the Knight is lost and Black can easily destroy the White without pawn before it promotes).

Alekhine temps Black to play gxh4 to stop the check, after which the pawns without are liquidated and the game is drawn. If Black plays ...Kh6, White can draw without by perpetual check. The players agree to end hostilities and the game is without drawn.
The game has transposed into a King's Indian Defense ("transposed" as ...g6 usually comes before ...d6).
Alekhine launches the dangerous Four Pawns Attack. It's evident that he's out for blood today!
This seems a bit passive.
White has built up a monsterous center -- his pieces and pawns control six squares of the fifth rank!
And with this move, Black sinks himself. The c6-Knight is not only a target (inviting d4-d5) but also blocks the c7-pawn. Now Black can't challenge White's center by playing ...c7-c5.
We see Yates' plan: to play ...e7-e5, supported by the d6-pawn and the two Knights.
Now Yates challenges the White center.
Better to take with the flank pawn than the center pawn.
Now Alekhine strikes at the nice target on c6.
And now we see why ...Nc6 just doesn't work in the Four Pawns Attack. Black needs to play ...c5 to challenge the center. Now Black is behind in development and White has a nice central pawn wedge.
When faced with an attack on the center, counterattack on the flank. Unfortunately, Yates picks the wrong flank. The moves ...f5 or ...Nf6 were better.
The idea is to double up on the c5-pawn after ...Qe7.
Alekhine sees through Yates' plan and makes sure the c5-pawn is covered.
The pawn is attacked three times and defended three times.
Yates prevents White from driving away one of the c-pawns attackers by Bg5...
...so Alekhine just picks off a different attacker.
Alekhine then sees a material-winning combination. First he thinks that if the c-pawn didn't have to be defended, it would free up his pieces. Then he sees what those pieces might do...
The Knight must retreat and no longer exercises control over c5...
...which allows the Bishop to do this.
Alekhine leaves the c6-pawn to its fate while he reorganizes his forces.
Yates' Rook pins the White Knight, but he's left the c7-pawn undefended.
Yates tries heroically to gain the initiative...
...but he can't get over on Alekhine, who masterfully defends while creating a threat of his own.
Yates sees there's no way to win back the Exchange, so he resigns himself to trading pieces.
Yates has the worse position anyway, but he just blows it with this move.

Note that even though Alekhine opened with the c-pawn, the opening has transposed back to a d-pawn opening (the King's Indian Defense). This transposition from a c-pawn  to a d-pawn opening is pretty common.
The Four Pawns Attack. This is White's most aggressive option in the King's Indian Defense and the most dangerous (for Black!).
Take a look at White's space advantage!
Black has to break the center before the White pawns become overwhelming.
Now the center is blocked.

Note the way both players are maneuvering for position. This is a characteristic of closed positions (ones in which the center is blocked by pawns) -- there are no immediate tactics, so both players try to get their pieces to good squares.
Alekhine later explained this seemingly mysterious move in his notes in the tournament book (see the variation).
Lasker cuts off the Queen's communication with h6, making Bh6 impossible for White.
Since the center is blocked, both players must concentrate on the flanks. Black makes his play on the Kingside, while White plays on the Queenside.
Note how quickly the pawns have expanded White's space on the Queenside.
Now we see the point of Alekhine's pawn sacrifice. But lasker has a trick up his sleeve.
The game very quickly became a tactical melee once the center opened up. Now we see the importance of getting your pieces positioned on good squares during the early maneuvering phase.
Black now has a chance to go after White's King on the wide-open board.

Black can easily protect his d4-pawn by using the Bishop, but won't be able to promote it (the White light-squared Bishop is the same color as the promotion square). He won't be able to force the h-pawn past the White King either (plus that promotion square, too, is guarded by the White Bishop). Despite being ahead a pawn, Lasker can't force a win.
Marshall (White) starts with a good opening pawn move. He now controls both without c5 and e5 and he releases the dark-square Bishop.

Reti (Black) counters by developing the Knight to its best opening square. By without doing so, he also keeps his choice of opening a secret to White, who doesn't without know if Black will develop his Bishops through the center or the flanks.
White develops the Knight toward the center, controls d4, and strengthens his without grip on e5.
Now Marshall knows that Reti intends to develop the f8-Bishop by without fianchettoing it to g7.

This pawn advance carves out some more of the center for White. Also, the b1- without Knight can develop to c3 without blocking the c-pawn, and the Queen has the without option to develop along the a4-d1 diagonal.

In the Hypermodern style, Reti chooses to attack White's center from the without flank rather than fight it out in the center with his d- and e-pawns. Once without the f6- Knight moves, the Bishop will attack White's d4-pawn.
Marshall gets the other Knight off of the back rank and into the game. Notice without how his pieces and pawns exercise control over all four center squares without (d4,e4, d5,e5).
Reti completes his Kingside development. Now his King is safely tucked away without and his Rook is developed toward the important center files.
Since Reti is allowing him to develop in the center, Marshall builds up an without imposing pawn phalanx by advancing the e-pawn.
This pawn advance prevents White from advancing either his Knight or pawn to without e5, prepares for a possible later e7-e5 pawn push for Black, and releases without the  c8-Bishop from captivity.

Marshall develops his light-square Bishop and gets ready to castle. But the without Bishop blocks the Queen's protection of the d4-pawn, which weakens the pawn without slightly. Perhaps 6.Be2 might have been better.

Reti's keen eye spots the d4-pawn's weakness and siezes the moment to exploit without it by pinning the f3-Knight. Now the poor pawn is totally unprotected! White without is forced to expend a tempo to protect it, or else...
...drive the Bishop away. Now the Bishop is forced to either withdraw or  without capture the Knight. This pawn attack is called "putting the question to the  without Bishop".
Reti decides to trade his Bishop for the Knight, insuring that the d4-pawn  without will remain weak and unprotected, at least for a while.
Marshall recaptures with the Queen, developing it in the process. This is without much better than doubling up pawns on the f-file with 8.gxf3. But now the without d-pawn stands alone...

...so Reti unleashes a discovered attack against it (from the g7-Bishop). without Despite the fact that he lags behind in development, Black still controls without the game by continuing to make threats which must be answered by without White.
Marshall protects the weak pawn and usefully develops his last minor piece at without the same time.
Reti hits the weak pawn a second time. How in the world will Marshall defend without it now?

He defends the pawn by advancing it! Now it's amply protected by two fellow without pawns and a Knight. At the same time he grabs more space on Black's side of without the board. Now c6 and e6 are unusable by Black.
The Knight leaps ahead and forks the Queen and light-square Bishop. See how without Reti continues to make threats and keep the initiative.
The White Queen retreats and simultaneously protects the menaced without d3-Bishop.
Reti hates to trade his well-posted Knight for Marshall's bad Bishop. But if without he doesn't, Marshall will play f2-f4 and drive the Knight back to d7, where without it becomes ineffective.

The Queen recaptures, but now it's not well-placed. See how the c4 and e4 without pawns block the Queen. Meanwhile, look at how much scope Reti's g7-Bishop is without  getting along the a1-h8 diagonal! Even though White's Queen and Black's without Bishop control the same number of spaces, the Bishop controls squares that without are much more important.
Reti develops his remaining Knight. Obviously, he's thinking about advancing  without it to e5.

Now that Reti has eased up the pressure, Marshall decides that this is a good without time to get his King out of the center. White's King is protected and his  without Rooks are connected on the first rank (and can support each without other).

Reti's idea is to try to win a pawn: after ...Ne5, White's Queen must move without and can't protect both c3 and c4. Depending on which square White leaves without unguarded Black will either play ...Nxc4 or exchange his Bishop for a Knight without and pawn.

Now c3 is defended by the Bishop. If Black plays ...Ne5, the White Queen can without retreat to e2 and White's position holds. Also, if the White Knight moves, without it uncovers an attack by the d2-Bishop against the Black Queen.
Black can't prevent the discovered attack, but he can keep the White Knight without out of his territory. The a-pawn advances, denying the square b5 to the without White Knight.
Predictably, Marshall uncorks the discovered attack against the Black Queen. without He also sets up a threat against Black's powerful Bishop. We'll see that without threat next move.

Reti has to retreat the Queen. None of the available retreat squares are very without good, but c7 is the least of the evils. On b6 the Queen takes a square away without from the d7-Knight, and on d8 it blocks communication between the without Rooks.
White challenges Black's domination of the a1-h8 diagonal. Marshall hopes without that Reti will decide to exchange the Bishops, thereby easing the pressure without on White's Queenside.
Reti pulls a rabbit out of his hat. The Knight blocks the exchange of Bishops without and menaces the White Queen as well.
Marshall's Queen drops back to the only square where it still protects the without weak pawn on c4.

Marshall surprises Reti by attacking the strong, centrally-placed Knight without instead of capturing the b5-pawn.
Reti springs a surprise of his own. The Knight is still well-placed on c4, without and it blocks the capture of the Black b5-pawn. But the exchange of Bishops without can't be prevented now.
Marshall finally has his way concerning the powerful Black Bishop. Now Reti without is forced to recapture to keep the material even. This hands the initiative without to Marshall.
Reti makes the neccessary recapture. Black's King is now slightly exposed and without White has the initiative. What will Marshall decide to do?
Marshall gets his Knight back into the game and re-connects his Rooks. The without Knight has gone from a poor position on d1 to a better post on c3 where it without attacks Black's b5-pawn.

Reti makes sure that his Knight will stay posted on b4, by making the pawn without push b2-b3 extremely unattractive to White (22.b3 Qxc3 23.bxc4 bxc4 and without Black is a pawn ahead or else 23...b4, where Black gets a cramping pawn without chain).
Marshall prepares a future a4xb5, which removes the c4-Knight's immediate without protection, and discovers an attack by the a1-Rook against the Black without Queen.

Surprise! Black's Rook comes crashing into the fight! Reti feels that White's without passed a-pawn could be dangerous later, so he keeps up the attack by killing without the pawn and getting the Rook into the game.
Swapping off the Rooks eases the pressure on White's threatened b2-pawn.
Black could have taken the Knight, but then he would have been behind by the without Exchange (down a Rook for a Knight). By capturing the Rook, Black keeps the without material even.
Rather than retreat his Knight, Marshall opts to trade it for Black's Knight. without Now, if Reti plays 25...Qxb5, Marshall can reply 26.Rxc4, as his Rook will without be protected by his Queen.
Reti captures the Knight as expected. He could also have retreated his own without Knight, but he prefers the exchange of pieces.
Marshall completes the piece swap. Now the ball is in Reti's court. What will without he do?
Reti makes another threat. This time he threatens to win a pawn and invade without White's position with 27...Qxb2 28.Qxb2 Rxb2.
Obviously. This was Marshall's only way to save the pawn. Now Reti can force without the exchange of Queens...

...which he does. Now Marshall must take with the Rook or be a whole Queen without behind (an overwhelming material disadvantage). See how Reti controls the without initiative by making moves that force a reply from White.

The material is even, but Marshall is now stuck with an isolated pawn on b2. without This pawn is very weak. Its weakness stems from the fact that there are no without pawns on adjacent files to help defend it.

The Black Rook advances to an outpost where it's protected by the c-pawn and without menaces two White pawns (b2 and e4). This ties up Marshall and restricts his without freedom of action, for if the e2-Rook moves, one of the pawns must without fall.
The White King begins its march to reach a square where it can protect one of without the threatened pawns.

The White King reaches a square where it defends the e4-pawn.
The Rook shifts position to another square where the c5-pawn still defends without it. It also sets up an "invisible barrier" on the d-file which White's King without cannot enter or cross.
Since his activity is now limited on the Queenside, Marshall advances his without g-pawn to grab more space on the Kingside.
Reti has a choice of two plans: to counterattack with his Kingside pawns or without continue to maneuver his King toward the Queenside. He chooses the latter.
Since the b2-pawn is no longer threatened, Marshall is free to prepare a without counterattack by moving his Rook.
Reti's Rook returns to b4 and attacks the pawn again.
Marshall, tired of being tied to defense, decides to abandon the pawn and set without up an annoying series of checks against the Black King.
Reti wins a pawn, but allows Marshall to counterattack with the Rook.
Marshall checks Black's King and drives it off of the back rank.
The Black King flees to the only possible square. Will Marshall decide to without check again, or will he attack the Black Kingside pawns with his Rook?
Marshall maintains the pressure by checking again.
The King escapes check and continues to protect the e7-pawn.
The White e-pawn advances, forcing Black to capture it (if Black doesn't, without then White plays 37.exd6 exd6 38.Rxf7 and wins a pawn).
Now Black is stuck with a weak, isolated pawn on c5.
White recaptures to complete the pawn swap. Now, if the White Rook moves, the without squares c6,d6,e6, and f6 are covered by White's pawns and are denied to without Black's King.

Reti hopes to strengthen the pawn by advancing it to a square where it is without easily defended by the Rook. Also, remember that a passed pawn becomes more without dangerous the closer it gets to the promotion square.

A centrally-posted King is a distinct advantage in the endgame. Marshall without moves his King toward the center, where it can move to the Quenside to help without attack Black's pawn, or to the Kingside to help prevent a Black pawn without breakthrough.
The Black pawn continues its march toward either coronation or death.
The passed c-pawn is a dangerous threat; if it manages to promote to a Queen, without White's a dead duck. Marshall is trying for a draw by perpetual check.
The Black King obviously must move to escape check.
Another check...
...and another evasion. The Black King must come back to d8 or else the without e7-pawn is lost.
Again, Marshall hopes to draw by either threefold repetition of position or without by perpetual check.
The King must move again.
Marshall again hopes to repeat the position...
But Reti will not draw quietly! He offers to exchange Rooks, forcing Marshall without to work for the draw.
Marshall surprises Reti with this move. The Rook attacks Black's passed pawn without (which cannot now be defended!).
Reti pushes the pawn, but to no avail. The pawn is marked for death.
Marshall springs a double attack (checking the King and attacking the pawn). without This assures the pawn's sad demise.
The Black King shuttles sideways toward its own pawns, in order to help without protect them or aid in their later advance.
Black's passed pawn finally gives up the ghost.
Reti wins a pawn using a basic tactic: the skewer, or x-ray attack. The White without King must move out of check, after which the Black Rook pockets the without h3-pawn.
The best place for White's King to move to. Now the King supports both of without White's center pawns.
Reti snatches the h-pawn. Now Black is a pawn ahead, and may have chances of without creating another passed pawn.

The King goes to the only square that still allows it to defend the without e7-pawn.

Marshall checks again...
...and Reti retreats. Rather than play out the moves for a threefold- without repetition, Marshall and Reti agree to a draw.
Gelfand plays openings which are ideal for an aggressive player, but he isn't a wild-eyed tactician; he's a planner and classical positional player.

White's aim is to open the e-file or to "break" Black's pawn structure. The immediate threat of e5-e6 is reminiscent of an Alekhine's Defense position. If White doesn't play e4-e5 immediately then Black might get sufficient control of e5 to keep White boxed-in on the light squares.
Black tries to keep control of e5 to prevent White from playing g2-g4 followed by Nf3-e5.
While Black gets good piece activity the poor pawn structure must make Gelfand a little nervous.

Playing a Nh4 or Nd4 to add pressure to the pin on Nf3 would be desirable, but White can step out of the pin with Qd1-e1. Black has to do more, so he castles and prepares to bring more forces into play.

Though White needs to clear the way for Bc1 to develop it's a little odd to see him weaken Nf3 this way. Does he intend to move Bc1 and then play Ne4-d2 to re-establish the defense of Nf3, or is g2-g4 still being considered?
White's pawn structure is quite modest, but from that his pieces might spring forward. Only the pin on Nf3 is troublesome.
It appears Black might want to play ...e6-e5 to secure control of d4 and f4, but he might also have in mind to play ...Bd6-f8 to keep the bishop on the board.

So, this is the idea behind Nd2-e4. Black has to either retreat and give up on the pin on Nf3 or give up one of the bishops for a knight. He could trade off Bd6  (13...Bxg3 14. fxg3) or Bh5 (13...Bxf3 14. Qxf3) .
Apparently he didn't see any immediate value to trading, so he keeps the two bishops in hopes of some future time when they'll be especially valuable.
I don't understand giving up Pc5 in this situation. What plan does Black follow which demands the bishop be at c7 rather than d6 or f8?
Black threatens to open the position, possibly with ...f7-f5, ...e5-e4, before White can complete his development.
White, apparently, is not terribly impressed and simply uses Pa3 to oppose Nd5 and possibly to support b2-b4, whereby Nc5 is defended and Bc1-b2 becomes available.
The resulting weakness at d4 seems trivial. The more important thing is to get rid of Nd5, so Bc1 can be developed to a useful square.
just keeping Pd4 defended, however awkward it may be
This clearly indicates he intends to get rid of Ne5 with his rook, hoping to retain control of f4 with Qd6 & Bc7.
Black has reached an impasse. His queen and rooks and even Bc7 are blocked severely on dark squares by Pd4 & Ne5.
White keeps Pd4 and Be3 to maintain control of the central dark squares.
White wins one exchange and now threatens two more! This looks like a catastrophe for Black.
saving one exchange and gaining time to save the other
At this moment it appears Black has made the necessary breakthrough. Be5 is a powerhouse and Rd3 is also very good.
White seems satisfied to repeat the position. Black may think he has the better of it, so he tries for more. I don't think that's a wise decision.
This move is what Black allowed when he refused to repeat the position and played 29...Re7. White now threatens Nc5xe4.

White is better on the queen-side and now has a share of the center under control (Bc5 & Pe3 work together well) , but Kg1 is a little exposed, so he should improve that before proceeding with his strengths.
activating the piece, preventing ...Nf6-g4+ and in place to defend Ph3
Black does all he can to avoid too many exchanges; he's also threatening Ph3.
How convenient for White, to end these exchanges by pinning Bf5!
unpinning Bf5 and threatening ...Bh3+ or ...Be4+ to win Rb5
Bareev has been a French Defense player for a long time. This may be the first non-French Defense game I've seen him play. He's a classical positional player, as is Leko!
White immediately goes after the exposed Bg6. This has been a normal move for many years now. The main alternative is to first play 6. Nf3, threatening Nf3-e5xg6.
Doing without h4-h5 has also been played quite a lot. Later on the Ph5 could be a weakness as it can quickly be threatened by ...Ng8-f6.

It always seems a little odd to see this bishop trade offer. Bd3 is White's better bishop, not conflicting with Pd4, but Bh7 is a very good piece and if Black puts all his pawns in the center on light squares then White's light-square bishop won't be better on any other square.

This is an interesting move which I've only seen recently. It essentially forces a weakening of White's queen-side pawn structure. In times past Black used to play ...Qa5-c7 and possibly aim for a bishop trade by ...Bf8-d6-f4xd2.

With Ph5 it's not so likely (though not impossible) for White to O-O, but with Qa5 it's not so easy for White to O-O-O. I think White would like to continue playing toward the center and see how Black's pieces develop before committing Ke1. But, Bd2 would be dominated too easily by a ...Nd5. The cautious alternative 14. a3, preparing c3-c4, just weakens White's queen-side further.

By itself the position of Black's queen should be some kind of warning that his position isn't going to become sufficiently active. Qd3 isn't defended, so there is still some possibility for Black to break out of the shell, but it could quickly become very difficult.
preparing ...c6-c5xd4. Earlier White could avoid the pawn trade with d4-d5.
White can't yet afford Bd2-c3 because ...Nf6-d5 (Pc4 is pinned) threatens Bc3.
Black wants to break up White's pawns, so he can use d5.
White's pieces are much better and Pc6 is very weak. The only question is whether Black can apply equivalent pressure to Pd4.

Black's position looks pretty good now. It's clear White wants to make something happen on the queen-side with his two-to-one pawn advantage and Black has to slow him down while making more of his king-side, mainly by grabbing Ph5.
Ra4 could be very awkward, perhaps even trapped by White's bishop and pawns.
This just begs for White to play b2-b3, forking Ra4 & Nc4.
Again, it appears Black is asking for trouble by allowing Re1-b1, pinning Nb2. Maybe he's just trying to distract White from capturing Pe6.
and it appears White has managed to capitlize on the pin!
though now the pin is reversed and Rb1 is quite awkward. If Black could get Pa7 to a3 or Nh5 to d2 then he might even win.
preventing ...Nf4-d3 from winning Bb2
defending Bb2, so ...Nd5-c3 can be met by simply moving Rb1
Rb4 is pinned on the file, so a trade is unavoidable. This makes it much simpler for White to win Pa5 and the resulting endgame.
This isn't the simplest ending to win. Pa4 restrains a minor piece and Pa4 isn't so easily gotten rid of.
The knight heads to c2 to control both a3 and a1. White needs to challenge the knight with either his king or Ne3 or Nd4.
Apparently Black is hoping to advance Ph5, particularly if White's king is too far afield, dealing with Pa4.
The threat to Pg5 by the long-range Bc1 has caused Black to retreat his knight all the way across the board.
going after Pa4
Black naturally wants to exchange off all the pawns, but he won't be able to.
Ne4 can catch Pd4 at d2, holding Pf3 at that same time, so the king catches Ph4.
After this White can establish Kd1 and Ng2 to keep Black's king from doing any damage.

From what I've seen Morozevich prefers stable pawn structures and depends upon piece play. He might like a Benko Gambit or a Dutch Defense, but in this case he's trying to provoke Bareev into 2. e4, an opening system Bareev doesn't usually play. This position could easily transpose to many different things: Dutch Leningrad with ...f7-f5, Gruenfeld with c2-c4 ...d7-d5, King's Indian Defense with c2-c4 ...Ng8-f6 and others.
This is usually followed by c2-c4 to make a King's Indian Defense, Fianchetto Variation or, after ...d7-d5, a Gruenfeld Defense.

This forces the game off into another direction. It's thematic for Black to fight on the dark squares, but White's setup is a little unusual. If White plays d4-d5 Black might play ...b7-b5; something he wouldn't ordinarily be able to do.
White chooses to support his central pawn and to block Bg7, but at the cost of not having c3 available for a knight. Incidentally, Pc5 is now threatened.
Black thre atens ...cxd4 to remove the central pawn. For White to simply defend it with Ng1-f3 is possible, but ...cxd4 cannot be replied to with c3xd4 (it's pinned) , so the central pawn is removed.
White uses a small tactic to get rid of Qa5, so Pc3 can truly support Pd4.
Black's queen is chased off the a5-e1 diagonal!
O.K. White has the central pawn, but Nb3 isn't terribly well placed. Black could go after it with ...a7-a5-a4.

Black chooses not to make it an issue immediately and develops more pieces. That's quite good because it's a recognition Black doesn't have to chase Nb3 and wouldn't necessarily gain anything from chasing Nb3 anyway; that Black can simply play normal moves and the weakness of Nb3 will show itself.

Audacious moves such as this aren't seen often. Black has traded his central pawn away and White shoves his to cramp Black, preventing ...d7-d5 or ...Nb8-c6. Black has to act forcefully to be rid of the influence of Pd5 or create some way to play around it.

Black is probably taking aim at Pd5 (though there is also ...Nb4 followed by ...Bc8-f5-c2) , but I think Black needs to ensure space on the queen-side for Qb6 and the knight by first playing ...a7-a5 and ...a5-a4 if possible.
essentially preventing ...Bc8-f5
threatening Bd2-a5 to win Qb6
It's odd to note this, but this is the same awkward place for the queen which occurred in the Leko-Bareev Caro-Kann game. Now Bareev is on the other side.
White just keeps moving forward into the breech and Black can't easily challenge any of White'spieces!

Though Black's position is generally cramped it's well coordinated and each piece, except perhaps Qa6, has a safe square to sit on. For White to gain some advantage he has to change that and perhaps advance his queen-side pawns or make some gesture toward the king-side (Kg8) .
A lot of White's advantage is dissipated by the piece trades, but the essential character of the position remains. Qa6 is badly placed and the c-file is an open avenue.

and Black threatens to maneuver the knight via e5 toward the queen-side where he might play with an extra minor piece, while Bg2 is useless! There is also the possibility, intended or not, of ...Bh6 to deflect Qd2 away from the defense of Ba5.
If White challenges the open file Black might play ...b7-b6 to open the a-file and capture Pa2. In that event it's likely both player's back ranks would become weak after a rook trade.
White tries to guard the weaknesses at b2 and c2, but it's clear now Black has more than equalized.
Black seems to be retreating toward his king, though I don't know why.
Black removes Pd5, so White's bishop might return to g2, mightn't it?
Black zeros in on the weak Pf2
But, before the bishop can do any harm Black will be able to grab it.
It's difficult for Black to find a good plan, despite his material advantage, because White's pieces are active and threatening Pf7. Black's Rf8 isn't of any use for the offense.

mate in 5. Notice that despite the fact all material is equal (except for bishop vs. knight) Black's forces are split into two groups which aren't working together, whereas White's forces are in one area and very much working toward one goal!
Though he has occasionally played this before it's somewhat interesting because usually plays 2...Nc6, often heading for the Marshall Gambit of the Spanish Game.
Essentially Black says White will have an isolated queen's pawn and Black will develop easily and then attempt to exploit his pawn structure advantages  (White's disadvantages) .
White is anticipating having an isolated queen's pawn and wants to avoid ...Bc8-g4xf3, undermining Pd4.
Finally Black feels it's safe, or necessary, to get rid of Pc4.

After this it's clear Black's plan is to occupy square d5, trade off White's light square bishop, occupy the central files with rooks and pressure Pd4. White has used h2-h3 to prevent ...Bc8-g4xf3, but Pd4 will be a weakness for some time. White, on the other hand, has use of Pd4 and the control of e5 it provides. Black's most dangerous piece is the one which can attack Pd4, so Bc1-g5, aiming to trade for Be7, might be very good. Perhaps White should encourage Black to occupy d5 (a2-a3 Nb4-d5) with a minor piece, so the file won't be open and Pd4 might be more safe. Then White could focus on occupying and utilizing the e-file.

It doesn't seem to me the queen does well here; it competes with Bc4 for light squares. The idea is to combine pressure on d5 with the threat to Be7. If Black has to use Qd5 to defend d5 then what defends Be7.
Now neither side has perfect pawns, but Pd5 might possibly be the weakest. At least Black has kept the e-file closed, so Re1 isn't terribly useful  (yet) .
further ruining Black's pawns and giving Bc4 room to retreat to b3, continuing the threat to Pd5
The c-file is now open, but there's no way for Black to invade at c2 (Bb3 controls c2) . On the other hand, White might try to invade to c7.

Black's pieces seem to have everything covered except e5. Next he has to figure out how to exchange pieces to lead to an equal endgame. White will avoid most exchanges, but how can he make progress? I suppose f2-f4-f5 is one way of disturbing the coordination of Black's position.

This appears to be chasing Bf4 toward a less useful square, but it might also serve to prevent f2-f4-f5. Unfortunately, for Black, it also shows up later as a weak point, not easily supported by pieces.
White has apparently decided he still has more chance for success via the e-file than anywhere else. How is he going to move Be6 off the file?

This seems odd to me. Of course, White doesn't have time for f2-f3 because ...Bxd4 is check, giving Black time to retreat ...Ne4-f6. But, it probably leads to a trade of dark-square bishops, something Black has been avoiding.
I don't see what Black gains by this exchange.

Can't anyone see why White is continuing to try to win, isn't it obvious he has tremendous potential? How can a Grandmaster achieve victories when he begins with this kind of position? Even Fischer, known for squeezing out points from such positions, had great difficulty against the better defenders of his day, such as Petrosian.
a slightly awkward place for the rook

Pg5 is hard for Black to support and White can simply push through over there, aiming eventually for g4-g5 to kick Nf6 away from the defense of Pd5. I know that may seem odd, since there are pawns in the way, but if Pg5 has to give way after h3-h4xg5 and f3-f4xg5, then White will indeed be able to put a pawn at g5.
In a general sense every one of Black's pawns is bad, but his pieces are wel placed to complement them. It's not so easy for White to make inroads.
White can try to chase Bc4 by playing a2-a4 (cutting off one retreat square) and then b2-b3. Bc4 is well placed, but can be chased to a horrible a6.
If White chases it now with a2-a4 the bishop retreats on the b5-e8 diagonal and Pa4 is suddenly a target! Incidentally, Black might now threaten ...Rc7-c4, hitting Nb4 and Pd4.

White is making a definite shift toward the king-side. I suppose he feels more confident of achieving something after g4-g5 and he wants to attack Black's king. Whether Black just exchanges pawns, opening the h- and g-files, or moves Nf6, there will be some room for White's pieces in that area. Black's rooks have to react somehow to oppose White's rooks.
White's dominance of the dark squares should remind Black of why he traded dark-square bishops, weakening his control of e5.
Lasker-Pilnik or Sveshnikov Variation
Now that Black has secured square d6, White can switch to taking aim at c7 and f6 by using Bc1-g5xf6 and Nc3-d5.
This is necessary to prevent White's threat.
White can defend Pe4, but he would be better off to capture Pf5 and not have a Bd3 which might soon be chased away by ...e5-e4.

After this Pe4 is immobilized (at least temporarily) . White doesn't want to move Nd5 away -- not that that would help after ...fxe4 and ...d6-d5. So, White continues quietly and hopes his king will be safer and the many weak spots in Black's position shall offer him opportunities for attack.
It seems to me Pd5 needs more support and White should play on the queen-side as part of that.
Black secures his king and eyes White's queen-side pawns while considering the ways White might try to attack at h7.

Black has methodically crashed through the queen-side and White has yet to get his king-side play started. Is Black winning already? It's possible. Pd5 is still weak and Black's rooks have open queen-side files, so all Black has to do to ensure at least a draw is keep his king safe.
Black prefers not to let Pe4 enter into the attack by e4xf5-f6. It also keeps Ne7 safe, so the exposed Bc2 is a big issue. The bishop is blocked by pawns on light squares in ever direction.
apparently planning Bd1-h5xg6 to undermine Pf4, but the recapture ...f7xg6 would uncover Rf8 to defend Pf4. I think Black is winning the ending if all the pieces trade. Pe4 is terribly weak.
White's position looks fine except for Bd1, it's blocked by pawns on light squares. So, while it may appear equal there are chances for Black to invade on dark squares and catch White wrong-footed.
threatening ...Qe3-g3+ and then ...Qe1+ to pick up Bd1

Now Bf3 is quite isolated away from Pa2, so ...Qe1-b1 and ...Ra8xa2 are possible. Only the threat to Pf7 is major. It takes Fritz 4 a while before it "realizes" how much advantage Black can get by using ...b4-b3 to open the a-file for ...Ra8-a1. Then it goes from an "equal" evaluation to decisive for Black!
White can't afford to abandon his king this way. But, perhaps he thought passive defense wouldn't hold a draw!
Black's queen does a good job of defending and attacking from this square.
White has no checks and Ne5 does double duty defending and attacking. The one thing Black lacks is Ra8, and Pa2 is enprise, so White needs to go back onto defense.
White has nothing more to lose, so he tries for a perpetual check.
48. Qg5+ Kf7 49. Qf5+ Ke7 50. Qe6+ Kd8 51. Qxd6+ Kc8 52. Qxb4 Rc2 -+ White runs out of checks and the Black rooks will help end it quickly.

This, the Caro-Kann, Advance Variation, makes a lot more sense for Topalov than the Classical Variation (3. Nc3 dxe4 4. Nxe4 Bf5) . He will have more opportunity to create complex, perhaps even confusing, positions. This suits his style and not Bareev's.

Black has a solid light square pawn structure, as in a French Defense, but with his light square bishop "outside" the chain. Black has spent one extra tempo  (...c7-c6) to achieve this. Is it worth it? Some people believe Bf5 is just an exposed target.
This is the very aggressive attempt to refute the early ...Bc8-f5. It's played before Black can use ...h7-h5 to secure the light squares even further.

Bg6 is blocked-in, Pd5 is weakened (in light of Bf1-g2 that's serious) and Pc5 is still en prise. After this move Black will have to keep an eye open for opportunities to play ...f5-f4 to reactivate Bg6. He might not want to do that when White can play Nxf4 and follow with e5-e6 to continue breaking up Black's king's protection.

At this stage of the game, and with the lines opening up, White has to take into consideration where his king will reside for the long run. Earlier he might have planned to O-O-O, but now that doesn't seem as likely. Pd4 prevents the simple Bc1-e3, Qd1-d2, O-O-O, so O-O seems more likely; and in that event it might be better to leave Pd4 to keep the c5-g1 diagonal closed. So, Ncxd5, O-O and Ne2-f4 followed by e5-e6 to further force an opening toward Ke8 seems to be the plan.

Black intends to get rid of Pe5 before it can be supported at e6, so White has to get rid of Pd4 to keep material equality or White can gambit Pe5, knowing the open e-file will be of use: 13. O-O Ndxe5 (keeping Pd4 defended) 14. Nef4

Black's central pawn chain is destroyed, but the knights have replaced them. Probably one of the knights has to be removed to weaken Black's control of the e-file. White has to make threats before Black can simply move ...Bf8 and ...O-O.
White sees ...Bf8-d6 as essential to Black's effort to secure Ne5, but after Nb5 there's less force available to break up the knights. It's a difficult choice for White. He chooses to threaten Nc7+.
It appears Black doesn't want to part with his dark square bishop, but that endangers his king.
White blocks Pf5 to keep Bg6 locked in!
It appears Black has survived anyway. Now he just has to figure out how to proceed without the use of Bg6!
threatening Nd5-f6+ to win Qd6
With Bg6 stuck it only makes sense to bring all the pieces into play.
He could be chasing Black's queen, just to see the positions, making it easier to decide which he prefers. Black will just stay active with his queen and take what he can.
White's pieces hold together as though they're glued.
This is a most interesting choice. The knight appears (despite immediate appearances that he's trying to grab Qe2 or clobber Pc2) headed to e6 to dislodge Bf4. White won't allow that, of course.
Now White has five pieces free to fight and Black only has three. Does it matter that material is nominally equal?
White guards g1 and offers a trade, knowing it's hugely to his advantage to trade pieces (except for Bg6) .
Though it's clear Black needs to activate Bg6 he can't afford to weaken his king in doing so. It might have been better to grab Ph4 before considering ...f5-f4.
clearing the way for Qd1-d4xg7#
Black doesn't really have any good moves.

Topalov puts an end to any hopes Black may have had of using Pf3 to stretch White's forces thin. After Nd1 Black may have lost by time forfeit, but he can't bring his king into play, Pf3 can't move and Pc4 can easily advance with the support of a king and two bishops (Nd1 holding Pf3 at bay).
French Defense, Classical Variation, He's hoping for e4-e5 to create a fixed blocked pawn structure where Black has ...c7-c5 to create queen-side play.

So, it transposes to a Rubinstein Variation after all. This has been quite popular among GMs in recent years, though Ponomariov beat Ivanchuk in the first game of their FIDE wch match. Black aims to not have any pawn weaknesses and to have a very secure king, hoping to trade minor pieces to achieve a draw. White has to fight piece on piece and be creative to force weaknesses in Black's position, so he can attack. To that end White has often, in recent years, aimed for Bf1-d3, Qd1-e2, O-O-O to bring the rook to the center quickly and to enable more free-wheeling king-side aggression.
Allowing Black to oppose both Ne4 and Bg5 seems to assure he will be able to trade several minor pieces to achieve the simplification he desires.
This allows White to maintain some tension, but would appear to commit the king to the queen-side. Black, on the other hand, is probably wondering if his king would truly be safe on the king-side.

Black usually aims to play ...Qd8-a5+ to get out of a pin on the g5-d8 diagonal. It helps in some cases to get rid of White's Pd4 to prevent White from having complete control of e5. It also limits Black's freedom to ...O-O-O and it takes a tempo away from piece development.
Without Nf3 to defend Ph4 White has to think twice about retreating Bg5-e3.
White takes control of the queen-side dark squares and Qd8 now appears exposed on the open d-file (after O-O-O) , so ...Qd8-e7 seems sensible.
I'm not so certain the knight is better here. It blocks the d-file and chases Qb4, but it also loses contact with d7, where it was useful preventing difficulties on the a4-e8 diagonal.
Black already has some difficulties.
Fritz 4 "thinks" this position is equal! That it doesn't "see" any problems for Kd7 is interesting. Topalov certainly saw possibilities.

This is an obvious, if highly risky, attempt to get Ra8 developed before Kc7 has to go back behind the pawns. Fritz 4 suggests ...Rh8-c8 and ...Kc7-b8, but what would become of Ra8? Black has to be very careful to properly balance his king's safety with attempts to achieve piece activity.
preventing ...Qe7-b4+. Ph4 is indirectly defended by Qa4.
Clearly both players see the queen-side is where all the action is to occur and they're bringing all their forces to that area. The exposed Kc7 draws a crowd.
There's no good reason to do this. It might not be immediately obvious, but the open area around Kc7 should have concerned Bareev -- on principle if not in light of concrete variations.
Topalov was not about to trade queens when he had a chance to go at Kc7 directly.
threatening Nxb5 to open the b-file

This move might seem a little speculative, but on principle Ka7 will never be safe and White's pieces have more open lines to go get him. Black won't have time to develop his rooks, so their value is almost nil, until you get a simplified endgame.

This at least wins Black's queen. Black hasn't maintained his king's safety and that lead to him having to defend rather than developing Rh8 and Ra8. Although White is behind a rook it's the one he has on b3 which is more useful than both of Blacks! It also helps that his king is rock solid safe.
Kasparov tries the Berlin variation, with which he had so much difficulty (as White) against Kramnik

Milos avoid s the usual 4. O-O to avoid whatever opening preparations Kasparov has made. Was this a prepared idea or a "spur of the moment" choice? Qe2 aligns with Ke8 and defends Pe4, so it should be alright.
After this White would be wise to not capture Pe5 because ...Rf8-e8 would give Black's pieces open lines and targets.
Black has little to worry about. He's going to have a convenient way to develop all his pieces and without having created any major weakness (es) .
I don't see Rd1 being very useful since Black hasn't played one of the variations with Be7 and his Qd8 isn't quite so cramped. It can easily sidestep the alignment with Rd1.
Black supports his central position and begins to aim for ...d5. He clearly doesn't fear White's approach.
This move admits the failure of Qe2 and Rd1. If he can't achieve Pd4 then Rd1 is bad.
This serves several purposes. One is to prevent b2-b4, thereby keeping Pb2 a little backward. It also clears the way for ...Bc8-a6 to target the weak Pd3 and Qe2.
a small tactical trick which may divert Black's attention from central play, but which does not gain an advantage
Black clears the way for ...Qa8 to support Ra4, keeping Pa3 backward and threatened. Black holds White's forces in place and hopes to be able to threaten them later-on.
incidentally threatening ...Rxb4 since Ra1 isn't defended
White might be able to play d3-d4xe5 after all. Pe4 is defended and can be resupported with f2-f3.
preventing d3-d4 and maybe considering ...c6-c5 to be rid of his doubled pawn.
White might like to play f2-f4, but he has to make preparatory moves (Kg1-h1 and moving Rd1 off the d1-g4 diag.) . Moving f2-f4 would help threaten Black on the king-side.
again considering ...c5 since Pb4 is pinned as Bb2 isn't defended Black could also have considered a simple maneuver of ...Nf6-h7-g5-e6-d4 to add more force at the center and toward the queen-side.
This move serves to begin a plan, but it's not without risks because Pc6 is left en prise.
Kasparov isn't satisfied to maneuver on weak squares he wants to provoke weaknesses around Kg1 and ...Nh5-f4 is certainly a threatening move which might provoke g2-g3.
Kasparov quickly scurries back to defend Pc6 and begins thinking of ways to maneuver to exploit the light square weakness around Kg1. White will have to act quickly to do something offensive.
not just defending Pc6 or pinning Pd3, but perhaps planning ...Qc8 to prepare ...Bd7-h3+
White has let his opportunity slip and now Black has his dark squares solidly defended. Bb2 won't be able to do much damage now.
All this dark-square activity is very good for Black. He's keeping Bb2 quiet and getting rid of his doubled pawn. Next will be an invasion on the b-file.
This keeps his king-side relatively safe. Pc5 will have to be lost, but Pa3 is also going to fall, so Black's heavy pieces will find plenty of activity.
White has an extra pawn, but Black's pieces are better. Pd3 is weak, Pb4 is weak and Kg2 is more exposed than Kg8.
He's trying to spin a mating net.
opposing Bh3 and hoping his king can survive the two Black rooks by sitting on f3
Pb4 will also fall, so Black is going to be up two pawns.
White released the threat to Pg7, so Black is free to go at Kh3 a different way.
One more example of how a super GM like Kasparov can outplay an ordinary GM as though it was Master vs. Amateur.
Queen's Indian Defense
Black has forced a slight weakening of White's queen-side and now he tries to discoordinate White's pieces.
It seems a little unusual to allow Bxb4 cxb4 when Black gives up on some central control. What he gains is control of c3, so White can't play Nb1-c3 to control both e4 and d5.
preparing Nb1-d2
Black doesn't worry about Pd5 blocking Bb7 forever. Since there's a Pc4 Black will have ...dxc4 to reopen the diagonal.

perhaps threatening cxd5 and Rc7 or Nc6, but as much as anything White is just moving forward into the gap and cramping Black as he goes. He might continue with f2-f4 to add another pawn to the central fight or e2-e4 to blast through the middle.
White threatens d5-d6 to win Bb7.
I think Black has used this rook to clear f8 if he needs to retreat his knight (...Ne6-f8) .

Black's queen-side coordination seems pretty good, but the possibility of f5-f6 to breech Black's king-side continues to give White the better chances to find a win. Incidentally, Pb4 is poison as long as Black has ...Rxc1+ to uncover a defense (Qe7 defends Pb4) .
If Black can get in ...Qc5 to force a simpler middlegame he would be fine.
Is Pe2 really the lynchpin of White's position? I doubt that capturing it is a significant to White as capturing Pd5 is to Black.
I can't see that the knight does anything productive here.
At this point Pe2 is defenseless, but Ba6 is hopelessly out of play.
and the threat of Rg5-g8# can't be stopped
Topalov is an excellent tactician and prefers the unbalanced fight this could produce.

Benko Gambit - Black uses Pb5 for one of several purposes: to get rid of Pc4 which prevents White from using central pawns to cramp Black, to inhibit Nb1-c3 because of ...b5-b4 and to open queen-side squares for the Black pieces, including Bc8 which might not be able to activate to f5 or g4.

Many moves have been tried; this one is useful without exposing to White the way White intends to play his pawns. For example, should Black play ...bxc4 and allow Nb1-c3 then White might follow with Nf3-d2xc4 with excellent coordination. Usually Black leaves Pb5 to maintain his options.
Black offers this pawn to open the queen-side further, expecting his improved piece activity to compensate for the pawn.
White refuses to cooperate and leaves Pa6 to block Bc8. Of course, he doesn't win a pawn this way either.
Black might plan ...Nxb6 to pressure Pd5, perhaps with ...Bb7.
threatening a4-a5 to hold onto Pb6, but weakening the b-file tremendously
Nd7 holds square e5 and Qb6 does better on the b-file than a Nb6 would.

At this point Black has an interesting choice to make. Some players have succeeded (as White) with a4-a5 and so some (as Black) have played ...a6-a5 and perhaps ...Ba6 to fight on the queen-side light squares. But, ...a5 weakens b5, so not everyone finds it appealing. But, what's the alternative plan for Black? Bc8 isn't developed, so ...e6 might soon be considered, but at the moment Pd6 is too weak for that.
It looks like he's just trying to trade pieces to ease his cramp, but this can be risky because White has mobile central pawns and is close to having them very well supported.

White decides he would rather leave the pieces on the board and fight for e4-e5 (a major strategic theme) or perhaps a direct king-side attack. Black has to commit to some other way of fighting actively.
to keep Na5 safe
and there it is Black commits to weakening Pd6 to force lines open. Fortunately this should be sufficient. White hasn't got enough of a lead in development (if any) to do any damage.

White switches to a policy of securing the light squares, and I'd guess moving Ra1, before even thinking of how to threaten Black's central pawns. This might give Black an opportunity. Na5 is only defended when Nc3 moves, but if Nc3 moves it exposes Ra1. Would Black trade Bg7 for Ra1? I think so. So, moving Nb6 to threaten Na5 has to be considered.

Typical Topalov, instead of applying pressure he opens lines for his pieces and then looks for weak spots where he can hit hard and fast. That this might simplify and allow his opponent to achieve equality isn't an immediate concern for Topalov.
The knight has moved and Ra1 is threatened, but Na5 is defended and Ra1 has time to move. What has Black gained (?) -- open lines!
With this great central piece activity you might think Topalov believes in Classical principles, and maybe he does to a certain extent.

This is certainly an interesting move. Is he planning ...h7-h5 and worries about a sacrifice at g6? Is he just playing a waiting move to gain clock time? I don't know how much time he had used to this point, so I can't know whether it was clock related, but I can imagine Black wanting to play ...h7-h5-h4-h3, slow as that is. More likely I'd expect Black to double rooks on the b-file.
After this Black threatens ...Bxc4 and White would have to recapture with a pawn, opening the b-file for Black's rooks.
Voluntarily weakening Kh1 isn't good, but the prospect of f4-f5 to open lines toward Kg7 must have been very tempting.
Winning one pawn is good, but trading queens might limit Black's ways of winning.
defending Ph5 and threatening ...g3 to remove another pawn from the cover around Kh1
Black defends Pg4, so he can play ...h5-h4xg3.
Black threatens ...Rxh2#, so White can hardly refuse to trade queens. But, there's a catch!
so that after 42. Kg2 Rg1# Tactical trickery at it's best: typical Topalov.
In some cases this restrains Pe4 sufficient to allow ...Ng8-f6, but in some other cases Black needs more control of e5.
Now Black has to decide how to prevent Nxc6 and e4-e5. To that end Black has played ...d6 (Scheveningen) , ...e5 (Sveshnikov) and ...Qb6 (Benko) . All have good qualities.
If White doesn't try to exploit the weakness at d6 then his pieces become too passive.
threatening ...b4 and preventing Na3-c4-e3

It seems odd that Black would allow such a pawn structure, but he can't easily be prevented from ...f6-f5xe4 to give him an advantage in central pawns. That the position has many weaknesses gives White room to develop and fight for a win.
After Ne7 it appears Black might prefer ...Bc8-b7, as is played in many Sicilian Defense games, to cut through the center of the board and to aim at Pg2, where White's king might soon reside.
Seeing that the piece needed to be improved and that d5 would be a good spot for it, she moves it now.

It might be a little unusual to use this move when Bg7 blocks the g-file, but Kasparov has played the King's Indian Defense many times and understands how to handle the weak d5 and the open g-file. In this case he might not aim directly for an attack on Pg2 and Kg1. Instead he might just be preventing Ne3 or exf5, so he can return to ...Bc8-b7 with either ...f5 or ...d5 soon to follow. Kasparov is very much about achieving good overall piece activity.
threatening ...Bh3 to checkmate with ...Qxg2# or to force g2-g3, so ...Bh3xf1 will win material and continue to weaken Kg1
These moves are very much taken from a King's Indian Defense player's repertoire.
Kasparov is always on the lookout for tactical shots which he can use to win or confuse the opponent.
offering Ra8 is just the sort of audacious thing Kasparov is noted for. But, don't think it's just a bluff. He's calculated variations to determine if his compensation is sufficient.
Material is nominally equal, but the exposed Kd3 could be a problem.
It's odd to see all these Black pieces cramped into the corner, but Black threatens ...Bf1 to win a queen!
It's a little surprising, after what had gone before, to see simplification; Black has a passed Ph7 and wants to advance it, so the h-file had to be cleared.

I suppose he's decided he can't just run Ph7 forward because Pc4 is also in good shape to advance and White's pieces might suddenly swarm Kg7. So, he has to continue the fight and await further simplifications when his king will be safer, then the pawns can advance.
prevents White's king from running to a2 (via b3) to get away from checks

clearing the way for ...f4-f3 and perhaps teasing Polgar into Nxe5?? Maybe Black has a won position anyway. White's pawns can't advance yet and with Be3 preventing Ra6-a7 there's no attack on Kg7. This is the moment for pawn advances.

Moscow Variation -- After this White will either establish a white square pawn formation (Pc4, Pe4) to replace the effect of the bishop (to the extent they can) or aim for c2-c3, d2-d4 and possibly d4-d5 or e4-e5. The move also works to enable O-O quickly. 3. Bc4 is interesting and has been played recently, but 3. d4 is still the most common move.
This is unusual, but not necessarily bad. If White captures Nc6 Black can recapture ...b7xc6 and have better central control. Perhaps Polgar is trying to take Kasparov out of familiar territory.
This makes Bf8 bad and doesn't prevent White from playing c2-c3, d2-d4 to open the center.
Already Black faces a crisis since White is better developed and Ke8 might soon be exposed.

This could be the move of a complete amateur or of a great player such as Ivanchuk, but it seems out of place and unusual, for Polgar. This may be a small indication of an internal struggle wherein she tries to expand her approach, hopefully for the better. In this case I think it just fails.
Opening the center is more important than the pawn he appears to be gambitting.
practically begging for ...d6-d5, so he can open the e-file with exd5
quite likely planning 12. e5 d5 13. Nd6+

Developing this piece to this square is usually normal, but in this case it's very strange. It helps keep the e-file blocked, but how are the king-side pieces to be developed and used? I'm not certain what Black's plan might be.
This position doesn't look too good for Black, but Na3 is misplaced and Nd6 is far from coordinating with other White pieces.
Kasparov just holds onto Nd6 and keeps an eye on how Black is going to proceed, looking for ways to gain advantage.
Pd5 is in danger of being captured by Na3-b5-c3xd5 and I don't see a very good defense for Black.

White takes over the center while Black squirms out of the corner. Is this sufficient to prevent White from crashing through the center? Well, first of all Pa7 is en prise, so White has to decide whether there is time to capture it and then return to the main theme.
Finally Black's position seems to hold together.
perhaps considering ...Bd8-b6, but also clearing e7 to develop Ng8-e7-g6

This position requires a comment. It appears Black has secured her king, but there's more of interest here. Black's advanced king-side pawns might give her a chance for some offense while it's not really clear White has any offense at all. The only factor which makes the position really murky is the blocked center. White has more space and Qd7 is dreadful, but can White actually penetrate Black's position? White can advance his queen-side pawns, but the king-side seems to be in Black's hands! This is an amazing realization to make after that peculiar opening. Perhaps a classicist would simply indicate that the immediate position doesn't appear winning for White, but Black will be compelled to make more moves and in so doing will unravel. We'll see.
chasing White's queen away from control of d4, so ...Bb6 can't be met by Nc6-d4
And, this is clearly too far-fetched.
Though Polgar has a rook on the h-file he would rather crouch behind the pawns than be flushed out to f1, or worse e2.

She wants to bring Qd7 to the h-file and/or to use ...f5-f4 to chase away Bg3, but king safety is the first priority! Allowing exf6 is extremely risky. If only there was another way, but I see none. I suppose this is where the classicist says, "I told you so." Black is having difficult with Qd7 because White dominates in the center, cramping Black quite a lot. So, when Black fights back those central pieces spring into action!
threatening ...Rxh2+ mating
forced, to avoid the checkmate
After this the position is changed dramatically and Black's king is in as much, or more, danger than White's.

This is a marvelous situation: Bf7 is pinned, Nh8 is stuck defending Bf7 and Qh7 & Rh5 can only sit on the h-file, but they can't open it. White has completely foiled Black's plan, but at a cost. The only question is whether White can finally get to the very exposed Kf8 because a failure to do so would probably allow Black to consolidate and win with her queen.
This looks like a time pressure move. It's quite ineffective. The threat is ...Qxg3.
After all that it seems terribly unfair that her heroic efforts to get active pieces was all dissipated, only to produce a losing ending.
Getting rid of the rooks makes good sense, as it makes the advance of Pg2 & Ph2 much easier.

Black loses her bishop after h5-h6 and Pg2 will keep Black occupied defensively while White's king gobbles Pd3 & Pa5 to clear the way for Pa2 to advance. This was quite an exciting game with the odd appearances and Polgar's heroic effort to gain piece activity, only to have it fall apart as they neared the time control (assuming that was move 40) .
